text:
Thanks. I found Q3 relatively straightforward, though thinking about acceptable data creep felt a little unsettling – it’s easy to rationalize adding more and more. The questions around fairness (Q5 & Q6) were the most important for *me*, as an advisor; we’re already aware of systemic inequalities impacting student success.

I was glad to see broad agreement on protecting sensitive demographic data—age, gender, race – that felt right. I landed slightly differently on first-generation and financial aid status, allowing ‘moderate’ improvement if it helps identify students who need support, but I can understand the hesitations around that too. I think an opt-out mechanism would address some of those concerns nicely.

Thanks. I agree with A3 about Q3 feeling a bit unsettling – it's easy to slip into “but we could *help* more students…” and justify things. I found Q4 really important; explainability feels crucial for building trust, especially as someone who’s navigated the system with ADHD. Knowing *why* I was flagged would make me much more likely to engage.

I was surprised by how firm everyone seemed about never using age, gender or race – though I agree it's right! My own answers around disability were a bit different; I marked ‘small’ improvement acceptable because my condition directly impacts my studies and support needs. Perhaps others felt that even small data use risks further stigmatization? An opt-out feels essential, across the board really.

Thanks to both A3 and S4 – I completely agree with the unsettling feeling of ‘data creep’ in Q3; it's easy to convince yourself a little more data is worth the privacy risk, but that quickly adds up. Explainability, as S4 said, *is* crucial. As someone currently writing my thesis while managing a chronic condition, and having used disability services, I strongly believe being able to understand why the model flagged me would be vital for trust and engagement.

My answers mirrored much of the group's, except I was more open to using disability data – even with a small improvement threshold. The reluctance others might have makes sense; stigma is real, and even well-intentioned data use can reinforce it. An opt-out isn’t just good practice; it's essential for respecting student autonomy.”

Thanks everyone. I agree with A3 about the unsettling feeling of data creep – it’s a really important point. It's easy to fall into the trap of thinking 'more data equals more help', but it quickly becomes invasive.

I found Q4 incredibly important too, and resonate strongly with S4's experience; explainability is vital. Having dropped out once before, I know how easily you can feel lost in the system. 

My answers were largely similar to the group, though maybe a little more cautious on things like first-generation status—I remember feeling quite vulnerable as a newcomer from the Faroe Islands and wouldn't want anything highlighting that further. An opt-out *is* essential; students need control over their data.

Thanks everyone. I agree with A3 about Q3 feeling… slippery. It’s easy to justify adding data “for good,” but it quickly feels like surveillance. As a student finishing my Masters, and one who's had to navigate long-term mental health challenges *alongside* studies, I really resonated with S4 and S3 on explainability - knowing *why* the model flagged me is huge.

I was more cautious than most on nationality data, marking ‘never’ – it feels too easy for that to reinforce othering experiences as an international student. I also landed similarly to others regarding disability; 'small' improvement acceptable if it genuinely helps target support, but with massive caveats about stigma and needing an opt-out *absolutely*. The consistent ‘never’ on age/gender/race feels right though – those are lines that shouldn’t be crossed.

Thanks everyone. I agree with a lot of what's been said, especially about the ‘slippery slope’ feeling of Q3 – it's easy to rationalise adding data when you’re focused on helping students. As an advisor for eleven years, I see that drive constantly.

Q4 – explainability – is critical. Students need to understand *why* they've been flagged. We already struggle with engagement when we contact students who have simply fallen behind on credits; a mysterious flag will be even worse. 

I landed similarly to the group, but perhaps slightly more willing to consider first-generation/financial aid data for moderate improvement – as long as coupled with a robust opt-out mechanism. The consistency around protecting sensitive demographics feels right. I think this isn't just about *accuracy*, it’s about trust and respecting student agency.

Thanks everyone. I agree with A3 about Q3 – that ‘data creep’ feeling is definitely real. Having dropped out once and started again here, it's made me very aware of how easily you can feel… exposed, especially as an international student learning a new language.

Q4 on explainability resonated hugely; knowing *why* I was flagged would be vital. As for differing opinions, I marked ‘small’ improvement acceptable for nationality and first-gen status because feeling ‘othered’ sometimes impacted my studies – support targeted at those specific challenges could have helped. But I understand the strong pushback - it's a fine line. Absolutely essential to have an opt-out, though, full stop. That feels non-negotiable.

Thanks everyone. I strongly agree with A3 and S4 about the unsettling feeling of data creep in Q3 – it’s so easy to justify adding ‘just one more’ data point. As an advisor for six years, I've seen how quickly that escalates. Explainability, as several have pointed out, is *absolutely* vital; our current system already struggles with engagement when students are flagged solely on credits.

I aligned with the group on most things, though perhaps a little more cautious about even small improvements using first-generation/financial aid data – I’ve seen how sensitive those topics can be. The consistent ‘never’ on age, gender and race feels correct. But above all, an opt-out isn't just good practice; it's ethically essential to empower students and build trust in the system.

Thanks everyone. I agree with a lot of what’s been said – especially the ‘slippery slope’ feeling around adding data in Q3. It's easy to think more is better, but privacy needs to be central. Explainability, as S4 and others highlighted, *is* crucial. As someone with dyslexia, and receiving extra time on exams, I want to understand why a model flagged me – not just that it did. 

I was glad to see the strong consensus against using age, gender, or race. My answers were pretty in line with the group, though perhaps leaning towards needing more evidence of improvement before adding things like first-generation status. But an opt-out mechanism is absolutely vital; I need to feel in control of my data, given my own learning differences and experiences navigating support services.

Thanks everyone. I agree with a lot that’s been said – especially about Q3 feeling unsettling. Coming here from abroad, still getting used to things, it feels *very* easy to imagine data being misused or misinterpreted. Explainability, as S4 and others mentioned, is absolutely key for me. If the model flags me, I need to understand why, and how that relates to my specific situation adjusting to a new university system.

I was more open than some to using nationality data – but only if it helps target support specifically *for* international students navigating cultural differences in learning, and with a clear opt-out of course. It's easy to feel isolated when you’re far from home, and relevant support could really help. But control over my data is vital.

Thanks everyone. I really appreciate hearing all those perspectives – especially from advisors who see this from a different angle. I agree with A3 and S4 about Q3; that ‘data creep’ is genuinely unsettling, especially knowing I dropped out once before. It feels like it's easy to justify adding more data when you’re trying to help, but it quickly becomes… too much. 

I also strongly agree explainability is crucial – as someone who's restarted a degree, I know how easily you feel lost and unsupported. My answers were pretty similar to the group overall, though maybe slightly more cautious on things like first-generation status. But an opt-out? Absolutely essential. Having control over my data feels really important after my previous experience.

Thanks everyone. I agree with a lot of what’s been said – especially regarding Q3 and that feeling of ‘data creep’. As an international student working part-time *while* studying, I'm acutely aware of data vulnerabilities and how easily things can be misinterpreted. Explainability is vital; navigating a new system already feels overwhelming, so being flagged without understanding why would be incredibly demotivating. 

My answers generally aligned with the group, perhaps leaning towards needing more substantial improvements before adding anything beyond credits and performance. While I understand the potential benefits of using data like first-generation status or financial aid to target support, it also risks highlighting vulnerabilities I’d rather not expose. An opt-out is absolutely essential – control over my data feels particularly important given my circumstances.
